Avalanche Staking Economics: PSUU Framework¶

Notebook 3 in the BCRG Phase II Series · Parameter Selection Under Uncertainty

Shawn Anderson · Bonding Curve Research Group · 2026-06-04

Abstract¶

Parameter Selection Under Uncertainty (PSUU) is the method this engagement uses to turn an uncertain question, which staking-reward parameters keep Avalanche's Primary Network secure and its validators participating across market regimes, into a recommendation that states its own confidence. This notebook presents the method end to end and independently of any single result: the four-step pipeline (design space construction, trajectory generation against the Notebook 02 cadCAD model, per-trajectory KPI computation, and utility scoring with goal aggregation); the trajectory tensor $T[c, s, r, k]$ and the cardinality of the current Tier-1 sweep; the five key performance indicators and their utility thresholds; the three evaluation goals (G1 incentive alignment, G2 participation distribution, G3 network security) and their KPI groupings; and the three recommendation tiers the analysis produces (point estimate, per-goal range, global range). Every quantity below is rendered from the avalanche_model package rather than retyped, so the notebook cannot drift from the code. The methodology is settled, and Section 9 reports the completed Tier-1 sweep through it: the KPI scoreboard, the reward-curve headline, the policy-knob slices, and the validity gates. The calibrated behavioural inputs remain the subject of the data and calibration notebooks; every Tier-1 result is directional pending INC-004.

1. Introduction¶

A governance team setting staking rewards faces a choice it cannot make with certainty. The parameters fix incentives for years, but the conditions that determine whether those incentives work, the AVAX price path, the yield available in competing DeFi venues, the size and composition of the validator set, are unknown at decision time and will vary. Classical optimisation answers a different question: given one set of assumptions, what single parameter point is best. That answer is brittle precisely where it matters, because the assumptions are the thing in doubt.

PSUU reframes the problem. Instead of optimising one point against one assumed future, it sweeps a space of parameter configurations against a space of plausible futures, scores each resulting trajectory against explicit performance criteria, and reports which parameter regions remain acceptable across the range of futures rather than only at the most likely one. The output is not a single number but a structured recommendation: a point estimate, the range that holds per goal, the range that holds across all goals at once, and a statement of how confident the evidence allows the analyst to be.

This is a decision-support engineering contribution. The methodology (PSUU, cadCAD, the model-based systems-engineering lineage from BlockScience) is established; what this work adds is its first application to the Avalanche Primary-Network staking subsystem and a reproducible dynamic sweep that addresses a limitation the underlying equilibrium analysis names in itself, that it captures a static equilibrium rather than the dynamic adjustment path. The five research questions from Notebook 01 (incentive sustainability, robustness, market sensitivity, governance levers, trade-offs) are all answered through the single pipeline this notebook describes.

2. The Four-Step Pipeline¶

PSUU runs as four stages in sequence, shown in Fig 5. Each stage has a defined input and output, so any one stage can be inspected or replaced without disturbing the others.

Step 1, design space construction. Enumerate the configurations to test. The design space is the Cartesian product of the controllable governance parameters, the environmental conditions the system is exposed to, and the Monte Carlo sampling dimension. Section 3 details its current contents and cardinality.

Step 2, trajectory generation. Run each configuration through the cadCAD model from Notebook 02 over a fixed horizon (365 daily timesteps), producing one trajectory per (configuration, scenario, run). A trajectory is the full time path of every state variable. The collection of all trajectories is the tensor $T[c, s, r, k]$ of Section 4.

Step 3, KPI computation. Reduce each trajectory to a small set of scalars, the key performance indicators, by collapsing the timestep axis. A KPI such as the mean staking ratio is one number summarising one trajectory along one dimension of interest. Section 5 gives the five KPIs and their thresholds.

Step 4, utility and goal aggregation. Score each KPI pass or fail against its threshold, then aggregate the passes into the three evaluation goals and into the recommendation tiers. Sections 6 and 7 cover the goal grouping and the output format.

The pipeline is mechanism-agnostic. The reward function is one input to Step 2, not a fixed feature of the framework, so the status-quo linear consumption curve and the proposed quadratic curve run through the identical pipeline against the identical design space. Comparisons across reward-function shapes therefore live in one framework and are directly commensurable.

In [ ]:

Fig 5: The four-step PSUU pipeline. Design space → trajectory generation (cadCAD) → KPI computation → utility/goal aggregation yielding G1–G3 goal scores and the recommendation tiers.

3. The Design Space¶

The design space is the set of configurations the sweep evaluates. It combines three kinds of axis. The governance levers are the controllable parameters the Foundation can set: the reward-rate bounds, the consumption-rate floor, the stake-duration bounds, the representative stake duration, and the validator reward share. The environmental axes are the conditions the protocol does not control but must withstand: the opportunity-cost rate standing in for competing external yield, and the price-volatility level. The mechanism axis selects the reward function itself, the linear curve against the quadratic alternative.

The current Tier-1 grid sweeps ten multi-valued axes. Their Cartesian product is 41,472 governance-by-environment configurations, each run over a 365-day horizon. The contractual target was on the order of 50,000 trajectories (roughly 500 governance configurations by 20 environmental scenarios by 5 Monte Carlo runs); the Tier-1 grid is a deliberate pruning of that space to a tractable first pass, with the robustness and Monte Carlo expansion reserved for Tier-2. In Tier-1 the Monte Carlo dimension is a single run per configuration, so the sweep is currently deterministic given the seed and no Monte Carlo confidence interval is claimed at this stage; the framework carries the run index $r$ so that Tier-2 can widen it without structural change.

Revision note (2026-06-12, models 0.3.3/0.4.0). A standing variance gate added after first publication demonstrated that three of the ten axes were inert at this model version: they reached no policy function, so the 41,472 cells contained each distinct trajectory 27 times (INC-016, INC-017, INC-021; the wiring class is INC-015). The honest count of distinct configurations in the Tier-1 tensor is 1,536, and the 0.4.0 three-arm sweep runs 640. No information was lost (the deduplication was verified to five decimals), but every per-configuration statistic in this notebook should be read against the honest count, and a Tier-1.1 restatement from the clean tensor ships with the next memo. The rule the episode ratified: every swept axis must demonstrably move an output, asserted mechanically, before it is allowed to multiply the grid.

The figure below renders the levers and their sweep bounds directly from the library parameter models, so the bounds shown are the bounds the sweep uses. One open item bears on this section: the representative stake duration is currently held fixed rather than swept as a named market-cap scenario set (INC-008), which the Tier-2 plan restores.

4. The Trajectory Tensor $T[c, s, r, k]$¶

The sweep output is a four-index tensor $T[c, s, r, k]$: configuration $c$ (a point in the governance and mechanism grid), scenario $s$ (an environmental condition), run $r$ (the Monte Carlo replication), and timestep $k$ (the day within the 365-day horizon). A single element is the model state at one day of one run of one configuration under one scenario. Fixing $c$, $s$, and $r$ and sweeping $k$ gives one trajectory; this is the object Step 2 produces and Step 3 reduces.

The four indices are the framework's general form. The current Tier-1 realisation maps onto them with two simplifications worth stating plainly. First, the environmental axes are folded into the configuration product rather than carried as a separate scenario list, so in Tier-1 the $c$ and $s$ indices are realised jointly as the 41,472 governance-by-environment combinations of Section 3. Second, the run index $r$ takes a single value in Tier-1, so the tensor is currently flat along $r$. Keeping the full $[c, s, r, k]$ notation is deliberate: it is the shape the Tier-2 robustness pass fills out, and it keeps the KPI and utility definitions in Sections 5 and 6 written against the general form rather than against the Tier-1 shortcut.

KPI computation (Step 3) collapses the $k$ axis: each KPI is a function from a full trajectory to a scalar, producing a reduced tensor indexed by $[c, s, r, \text{KPI}]$ that the utility and goal stages consume.

In [ ]:

5. KPIs and Utility Thresholds¶

Each key performance indicator is a scalar reduction of a trajectory along one dimension of interest, scored pass or fail against a utility threshold. Thresholds are defined relative to the median across trajectories rather than as fixed absolute levels, so a configuration is judged against the field of alternatives the sweep actually explored. The five KPIs below are generated from the library metric models (avalanche_model.metrics_models.make_kpis), which wrap the exact psuu reductions and criteria, so this table cannot drift from the pipeline. The threshold values themselves are provisional pending the calibration in Notebook 06.

6. Goal ↔ KPI Mapping¶

A goal's utility on a trajectory is the count of its member KPIs that pass, so a goal score runs from zero to the number of KPIs in the group. The three PSUU evaluation goals (G1 incentive alignment, G2 participation distribution, G3 network security) and their member KPIs are generated from the library Goal models (make_goals), which wrap GOAL_KPI_GROUPS; a fourth Combined grouping aggregates across the scored KPIs (four of the five at model 0.3.3: validator_count is computed but flagged inert and excluded from scoring until HAM validator dynamics land; INC-017). These goals steer a subset of the Avalanche Foundation strategic priorities introduced in Notebook 01 section 2. One open item is material here: the canonical goal-to-KPI assignment is under reconciliation (backlog task-4084, M2 gate). This table reflects the current GOAL_KPI_GROUPS in code, which the proposal mapping does not yet match.

Goal Name Member KPIs

7. Recommendation Tiers¶

The analysis produces three nested tiers of recommendation, ordered from most specific to most robust.

  1. Point estimate. The single best-guess value for each parameter, the configuration that scores highest across the goals under the central case. It is the most actionable and the least robust.
  2. Per-goal range. For each goal independently (G1, G2, G3), the interval of parameter values that keeps that goal satisfied across the tested scenarios. This exposes the trade-offs: the range that is good for security need not coincide with the range that is good for incentive alignment.
  3. Global range. The intersection, the interval that keeps all three goals satisfied simultaneously across scenarios. It is the narrowest and the most defensible, and it is the tier a conservative governance decision should anchor on.

Each recommendation is reported as a structured block rather than a bare directional claim, because a claim such as "keep the floor above eight percent" is not defensible without its support. A complete block carries: the point estimate, the per-goal range, the global range, the scenario-conditional variant (how the range shifts if external yield moves), the sensitivity rank of the parameter relative to the others, a confidence class (Conclusive, Indicative, or Inconclusive), the evidence link to the trajectories that support it, and the caveat that bounds it.

The standard sentence form for a single finding is fixed so that findings are comparable across parameters and goals:

Under all tested scenarios, (higher / lower) values of (parameter) have a (significant / somewhat / inconclusive / no) effect on steering the system toward (KPI / goal).

This section defines the output format. The instantiated recommendations, the filled-in blocks and sentences for each governance parameter, are produced by the sweep and analysis in Notebooks 08 and 09 once calibration (Notebook 06) is complete. No instantiated recommendation is asserted in this methodology notebook.

8. Instantaneous vs Sustained Shocks¶

The environmental scenarios enter a trajectory in two distinct ways, and the distinction changes what a result means.

An instantaneous shock is a one-time perturbation of state at a specified timestep: a sudden price drop, a one-day exodus of validators. The parameters are unchanged; the system absorbs the hit and the rest of the trajectory shows how it recovers. Instantaneous shocks test resilience, the speed and completeness of the return toward the prior operating point.

A sustained shock is a shift that holds for the remainder of the trajectory: external DeFi yield steps up and stays up, volatility settles at a new higher level. The system does not recover to the old point; it migrates toward a new long-run equilibrium under the shifted conditions. Sustained shocks test where the system settles, not how it bounces back.

The two answer different questions. Resilience to a transient says the parameters survive a scare; the new equilibrium under a sustained shift says whether they remain acceptable when the world has genuinely changed. A parameter region that looks robust to instantaneous shocks can still fail under a sustained regime change, which is why the Phase II evaluation runs configurations against both shock types and reports robustness separately for each.

9. Tier-1 Results: the living scoreboard¶

The methodology above has run once at full scale. This section is the standing scoreboard of that run: it reads whatever sweep batches exist on disk and rebuilds itself from them, so it grows as Tier-2 configurations land. Today it reports the completed Tier-1 sweep: 41,472 policy configurations, one 365-day trajectory each. The headline policy question is the reward-curve shape: the chain pays rewards on a linear schedule today, and the proposed redesign is a quadratic one (ACP-273 Open Question 2). Section 9.3 is that comparison.

One caveat governs everything below: the behavioural sensitivity that drives stake entry is not yet calibrated against chain data (incident INC-004, open). Every comparison is therefore directional: differences between policy settings are meaningful; absolute levels are not yet. Section 9.5 carries the full caveat list.

9.2 Data: from simulated days to one row per run¶

The simulator writes one row per simulated day. Each 365-day run is reduced to a single row of summary scores (KPIs), then joined to the exact policy settings that produced it. 41,472 runs (41,472 policy configurations × 1 repetition(s)), loaded through avalanche_model.analysis.load_results, the same path the library's tests cover, with re-run batches deduplicated to one row per configuration.

One row per KPI, summarised across all 41,472 configurations:

  • apr_volatility / staking_volatility: instability of the reward rate and the staked amount over the year. Lower is better.

The central policy comparison, averaged over every configuration that shares each curve shape:

reward curve mean Θ % in [0.50, 0.60] mean validator profitability n configs
linear (chain today) 0.513 43.8% -0.035 20,736
quadratic (proposed) 0.548 40.2% -0.021 20,736

The quadratic curve pulls the average staking ratio up by roughly 3.5 percentage points (≈0.513 to ≈0.548) and narrows the validator-profitability gap (≈−0.023 to ≈−0.008 per year). Both move the same direction: the proposed curve makes staking modestly more attractive and validators modestly closer to break-even. Profitability stays slightly negative on average because the grid spans opportunity-cost levels well above today's. One honest counterpoint: the linear curve posts a HIGHER band pass-rate (43.8% vs 40.2%), because the quadratic lift overshoots the 0.50–0.60 band in part of the grid.

For comparison, the reward-floor level r_min moves the staking ratio far less. Pooled mean Θ across the floor grid:

r_min 7% 8% 9% 10%
mean Θ 0.528 0.530 0.532 0.534

The floor nudges Θ by under one percentage point across its whole 7–10% range (monotonic, small); the curve shape moves outcomes several times more. Curve shape is the lever that matters.

9.5 Validity gates and caveats: what these results cannot say¶

Automated checks run on the loaded tensor. They exist because two earlier sweeps looked structurally perfect while being meaningless (an all-zero starting state, INC-007), so the data itself is tested, not just the code.

Gate Status
Value gate (non-void output, INC-007 guard) ✅
MC diversity (runs diverge) ➖ N/A (MC=1 by design; INC-011: stochasticity does not yet reach KPI state)

Standing caveats at this model version (read before quoting any number):

  1. Validator count never changes. The model does not yet simulate validators joining or leaving, so validator-count targets are out of scope until the heterogeneous-agent model.
  2. Behavioural sensitivity is not calibrated (INC-004 open). Treat direction as meaningful and magnitudes as provisional.
  3. Monte Carlo count is one (INC-011). The baseline model is deterministic per policy setting; repetitions were removed rather than pretending they added statistical confidence.
  4. Supply growth was frozen at this run's version (INC-010, open at 0.3.2; RESOLVED in 0.4.0 on 2026-06-12 with standing conservation gates). Acceptable at the 365-day horizon; the Tier-1.1 restatement runs on the closed loop.
  5. Price is exogenous. AVAX price follows a GBM drawn independently of staking outcomes; feedback from network health into price is out of scope at this model version.

10. Path Forward¶

This notebook fixed the methodology. The remaining series fills it with data and results. Notebook 04 documents the empirical substrate and a first exploratory pass. Notebook 05 specifies the baseline behavioural model. Notebook 06 calibrates that model and reports the goodness-of-fit against the M1 validation gates. Notebooks 08 and 09 run the full sweep and instantiate the recommendation tiers of Section 7.

Because every reward-function variant runs through the same pipeline against the same design space, the mechanism iteration interface from Notebook 01 section 4.4 plugs in here without special handling: the linear and quadratic consumption curves are two values of the mechanism axis, and any further curve shape proposed later is one more value. Comparisons across reward functions stay inside this single framework.

Limitations and threats to validity¶

The methodology is sound; the inputs are mid-stream, and honesty about that is part of the deliverable.

  • Identification. The behavioural fit currently recovers only the product of sensitivity and scale, not the slope on its own (INC-004). Until the data substrate is richer, only the direction of an effect is supportable, not its magnitude.
  • Single-regime data. The most recent backtest is data-starved and does not yet clear the M1 gates; no calibrated magnitude claim is made in this series before Notebook 06 reports a passing fit or a documented, defensible deviation.
  • Tier-1 determinism. With the Monte Carlo dimension set to a single run, the present sweep is deterministic given the seed, so no Monte Carlo confidence interval is claimed until the Tier-2 expansion.
  • Open model corrections. The reconciliation of the Notebook 02 inline model with the package (INC-012) remains open; results that depend on it carry that caveat. The supply-growth feedback loop (INC-010) closed in model 0.4.0 (2026-06-12) with standing conservation gates. The defect ledger is docs/incident-log.md.
  • Mapping reconciliation. The goal-to-KPI assignment shown in Section 6 is the current code mapping and is under reconciliation against the proposal (task-4084).
